turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Doctor. I did the lying and standing pressures before she came in. Lying was 156 over 84, pulse 72. Standing, after a minute, 118 over 76, pulse 94.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Mrs Pillay, have a seat. Your daughter can stay. Dizzy, is it?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor, I'm so worried. When I stand up the room goes funny, like I'm on a boat. I didn't really fall, though. I just slid.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ma, you did fall. Twice. Once in the passage and once by the stoep. You ended up on the floor both times.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Ag, it wasn't a proper fall. My legs just went and I slid down on my bum. I didn't hit my head, I don't think. Did I?
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You didn't hit your head, no. But you were down, properly down, and the second time you bruised your right shin. She keeps saying it was nothing.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has the giddiness been going on?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, the giddiness, two weeks, or maybe a bit more. The first time I slid I can't pin, last winter or the one before. I really can't say.
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's longer than two weeks, Doctor. She's been giddy on standing since before Christmas. I'd say a good two months. She just plays it down.
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Two months? Shame, I don't know, it feels recent to me. I'm anxious about it, that's all. Is it a stroke? My neighbour had a stroke.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not jumping to that. Did you black out?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No, I never lost consciousness. I was awake the whole time, both times.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's true. She was talking to me. No blackout.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No chest pain.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Headache?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): No headache. Just the giddy feeling, and then I'm tired after. Is tiredness a bad sign?
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll come to that. Any palpitations?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): No, my heart doesn't race. Well, actually, when I stand it feels thumpy, but not really racing. I'm not sure.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nausea? Vomiting?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): No vomiting. A bit queasy sometimes when it's bad, but I haven't been sick.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): You take blood pressure tablets.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes. Amloc in the morning. I think it's 5 milligrams. And the water tablet. And at night the sleeping one.
[SEG0026] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The Amloc box at the flat is 10 milligrams, Ma, not 5. I've seen you take one every morning. Don't tell the doctor the wrong dose.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Is it 10? I always thought it was 5. Now I'm all confused. Which is it?
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll sort the dose. Don't guess. What is the water tablet?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): I just call it the water tablet. The little white one that makes me pee. I don't know the proper name.
[SEG0030] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's Ridaq, 25 milligrams, one in the morning with the Amloc. For the blood pressure. She's been on it for years.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the sleeping tablet. Name?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Um. The little white sleeping tablet. I can't remember what it's called. Stilnox? Or is that something else?
[SEG0033] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I think it is Stilnox, but I'm not a hundred percent. The bottle's at home. She takes one at bedtime, most nights.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes I take half if I'm already dozy, or a whole one. I honestly don't know what I did last night. Is that dangerous, should I stop it tonight?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): One thing at a time. High blood pressure for how long?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Years. Ongoing. The clinic put me on tablets ages ago.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Diabetes?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart attack, stroke, Parkinson's?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): No, none of that, thank goodness. My mother had blood pressure, though. Is it hereditary? Will I end up like her?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Common. Doesn't change today's plan. Do you live alone?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, in my flat in Pietermaritzburg. My daughter comes past most evenings. I'm frightened to shower now. What if I slide in the bathroom?
[SEG0043] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I've been sleeping on the couch since Tuesday because I don't trust her on her own at night. She hates that I say it.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Smoking? Alcohol?
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't smoke. Never have. A glass of wine at Christmas, that's all. Hardly counts, hey?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at that shin.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bruise on the right shin, yellowing, skin not broken. No swelling of the ankle. Pulse in the foot is fine.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): Is the bruise a clot? Do I need a scan of the leg? I'm so worried about clots.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's a bruise, not a clot. I'm going to stop the Amloc. That drop when you stand is from the blood pressure tablets.

[SEG0050] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Before you do that, Doctor, she also gets up at night to pee a lot since the water tablet, and the giddiness is worst first thing after the tablets. And she didn't tell you she nearly slid again yesterday morning.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): Yesterday was nothing, I held the kitchen counter and I didn't even go down. Please don't take all my tablets away, my pressure will shoot up. What will happen to me?
[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to interrupt. I rechecked the standing pressure just now because she stood up fast in the passage. It was 104 over 68, pulse 102. She had to sit.

[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): All right, scratch the Amloc change. I'm leaving the Amloc until we see the box, and I'm stopping the water tablet, the Ridaq, from today. That drop fits the water tablet better.
[SEG0054] person_3 (PATIENT): Stop the water one completely? Not just half? What if my ankles swell? They swelled last winter, or maybe the winter before, I can't remember which.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the ankles puff up, we deal with it then. For now the Ridaq goes. Keep taking the Amloc every morning, whatever strength is on the box. Bring the box next time.
[SEG0056] person_3 (PATIENT): And the sleeping tablet, do I take it tonight? I'm scared I'll be woozy and fall. Can I take half, is half safer?
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the sleeping tablet as you have been for now. Don't fiddle the dose tonight. We might cut it later if you're still unsteady, but not today.
[SEG0058] person_3 (PATIENT): So no hospital? I don't have to sleep here? My bag isn't even packed, and Thandi's bakkie is on the yellow line by the robot.
[SEG0059] person_2 (DOCTOR): No admission. I was going to send you for a CT of the head today, given two falls.

[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): Actually no. You didn't strike your head, you didn't black out, and the pressures explain the giddiness. We might do a scan if it hasn't settled once the water tablet is out. Not today.
[SEG0061] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should she have blood tests? Her last ones were at the clinic ages ago. I don't know when.
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'll order a urea and electrolytes and a full blood count today. Sister can take the blood before you leave.
[SEG0063] person_3 (PATIENT): Will the needle hurt? I'm terrible with needles. And what are you looking for? Is it my kidneys?
[SEG0064] person_2 (DOCTOR): Kidneys and salts, because of the water tablet, and a blood count. It's a quick blood draw.
[SEG0065] person_3 (PATIENT): What if I get dizzy in the shower? Must I sit? Should someone be there? I'm really anxious about the bathroom.
[SEG0066] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sit to wash. Don't lock the door. Stand up slowly and count to ten. If you feel yourself going, sit on the floor.
[SEG0067] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll stay the nights until the next visit. She won't ask, but she needs it.
[SEG0068] person_3 (PATIENT): You don't have to, Thandi, you've got work. But... please do. What about my pressure going high if I stop the water tablet? How high is dangerous?
[SEG0069] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll recheck. Come back in two weeks for the standing pressure. Not before, unless you black out or you can't stand at all.
[SEG0070] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks is a long time. What if I slide again tomorrow? Do I come back or phone? Is it an emergency?
[SEG0071] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you go down again or the giddiness is worse, phone the rooms or come in the same day. Don't wait the two weeks for that.
[SEG0072] person_3 (PATIENT): And the scan, you said maybe a scan. Is that booked? I'm confused what is happening and what isn't.
[SEG0073] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing is booked for a scan. We might do one only if you're still giddy at that two-week visit. Clear?
[SEG0074] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring the Amloc box and the sleeping-tablet bottle so you can see the names and the doses. She mixes them up.
[SEG0075] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Sister, bloods before they go. Lying pressure was already done; no need to repeat it.
[SEG0076] person_1 (NURSE): I'll take the bloods now. Mrs Pillay, it'll be one little needle, then you're done.
[SEG0077] person_3 (PATIENT): Okay, sorry I ask so much. I just don't want to fall and be a burden. Thank you, doctor. Thandi, don't let me forget the boxes.
